We've seen multiple examples of why giving Meta's Muse app full disk access on a Mac is a terrible idea, and now another major privacy issue has surfaced. The latest discovery shows that Muse analyses your communications with everyone in your life every single hour.

Apple has expressed serious concern about the development, stating in a blog post that it will introduce more controls around the "Full Disk Access" feature, which is the very thing that has caused these problems...

Meta Muse app prompts swift action from the authorities

Meta recently launched Muse, its personal AI agent app, for iPhone and Mac. Despite the obvious foolishness of giving a Meta app unrestricted access to everything on your Apple device, it quickly reached the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, things soon went badly wrong, and the situation hasn't improved since. Wired reports that security researcher Karan Joshi found that Meta had instructed Muse to harvest all the data needed to build a complete map of every relationship in your life.

One of Muse's instructions appears to be to create "a page for every person" in the user's life. The instructions state the hourly process involves organising data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "partners," and people you "follow"… "where they live, what they do, recurring topics (apartment hunting, joint savings goals)," the instructions read. They add that the model may also note "important dates" such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history file could include context like "the March trip, the argument that was later made up, last week's milestone."

Apple tightens up use of Full Disk Access permissions

You might think the prompt asking for Full Disk Access on a Mac speaks for itself, but that doesn't seem to be the case. Even tech-savvy users are handing over this unrestricted pass to their computers without fully understanding how dangerous it is.

Apple says the feature was originally intended for backup apps, but developers are now using it for a much wider range of purposes, including AI agents. The company has said it intends to "introduce more controls" to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when granting this permission.

Here's what Apple must do — and absolutely should not do

Apple says taking such measures is "critical," and I couldn't agree more. Since the current permission requests don't adequately convey the gravity of granting this access, Apple must ensure users truly understand what they're allowing.

What I'd like to see is much clearer text urging users not to grant the permission unless they're sure of the consequences. Something along the lines of:

Basically, the wording can't be too strong. And for apps that have already been granted this access, I'd welcome a one-time prompt asking them to reconfirm.

Peter's comment has received the most likes

While I find Apple's occasional notifications asking whether I want to keep letting apps access my location a bit annoying on iPhone, I do appreciate it. At least once, I realised I didn't want an app to have that level of access any longer. It also reminds me to periodically think about what other apps might be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat the mistake it made with screen recording permissions in macOS Sequoia. Granted, that's an extremely dangerous setting too, and a stern warning is justified, but Apple's approach back then was to force us to reconfirm these permissions every week and every time after a restart.

The move was widely criticised for turning macOS into Microsoft Vista, forcing users to endure "a subscription service you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, Apple already goes too far on iPhone with occasional permission reconfirmations. For example, I've authorised Citymapper to access my location so it can keep giving me navigation in the background, and Apple, I really don't need you asking me again whether I still want that setting.

Yes, the strongest possible warning should be issued when granting Full Disk Access, but if someone chooses to do so, macOS must respect that decision. No more weekly or periodic mandatory reconfirmations, thank you.
